Q: Why does Groq langchain model return 'tool use failed error'? A:

The error is coming from Groq's API, not from your tool code. Look at the failed_generation field:

'<function=addTopic{"Topic": "Python Lists"}</function>'

The model is generating a malformed tool call — it's outputting that XML-like string instead of a proper structured tool call. Groq's API rejects it before your function ever runs, which is why print() inside the tool shows nothing.

There are two things causing this:

1. Your docstring is doing too much

The tool docstring should describe what the function does and what arguments it takes. Yours is full of instructions about when to call it, how topics relate to the database schema, why TopicID is NULL, etc. That's system prompt territory. When the tool description is this noisy, Llama models on Groq tend to choke on the structured output and fall back to generating that raw <function=...> string instead.

2. The parameter name is uppercase

Topic:str (capital T) is unusual for a Python function signature. LangChain builds the JSON schema from it, and Llama models are sensitive to non-standard parameter naming in tool schemas.

Fix both:

@tool
def add_topic(topic: str) -> str:
    """Add a new coding topic to the database."""
    connection = sqlite3.connect("learn.db")
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "INSERT INTO TOPICS(TopicID, Topic, Understood) VALUES(NULL, ?, 'False')",
        (topic,)
    )
    connection.commit()
    connection.close()
    return f"Added topic: {topic}"

Key changes:

  • snake_case function name (LangChain uses this as the tool name in the schema)
  • lowercase parameter name
  • docstring is one line — just says what it does
  • returns a string (LangChain tools should return something; returning None can confuse the agent loop since it doesn't get confirmation the action succeeded)
  • parameterized SQL instead of f-string (your original was a SQL injection vector)

Move all the behavioral instructions into the system prompt where they belong:

agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[gen_questions, add_question, add_topic],
    system_prompt=(
        "You are a helpful coding tutor. "
        "Ask the user what Python topic they'd like to cover. "
        "Use add_topic to store the topic, then use gen_questions to create 5 questions. "
        "Each question should be repeated until answered correctly. "
        "Topics should be specific Python concepts, not broad generalisations. "
        "Progress from easier to harder topics based on user performance."
    )
)

To answer your architecture question: no, you don't need to define search queries yourself. The LLM decides when and how to call tools based on the system prompt and tool descriptions. But it can only do that reliably when the tool schemas are clean and the instructions are in the right place (system prompt for behavior, docstring for what the function does).

Also — one thing to be aware of with llama-3.3-70b-versatile on Groq specifically: if you have more than ~4-5 tools with long descriptions, tool calling gets flaky. Keep descriptions short and tool count low.

Q: How to both fetch all Kubernetes objects as a snapshot and stream changes? A:

The 410 Gone error is happening because you're storing the maximum resourceVersion from individual objects in the list response. That's the wrong version to use. Kubernetes compacts its watch history (etcd revisions) aggressively, and by the time you start the watch, that per-object version is already behind etcd's compaction watermark.

The fix is simple: use the resourceVersion from the list response metadata, not from individual items. That version represents the point-in-time of the list operation itself, and the API server guarantees it's valid as a watch starting point.

# Step 1: List (snapshot)
response = await api.list_custom_object_for_all_namespaces(
    self._group, self._version, self._kind
)
# This is the version you want — it's on the list response, not on individual items
list_resource_version = response["metadata"]["resourceVersion"]

# Process your snapshot
for item in response["items"]:
    self._cache[item["metadata"]["name"]] = item

self._ready = True  # snapshot complete

# Step 2: Watch from that exact point
w = watch.Watch()
async for event in w.stream(
    api.list_custom_object_for_all_namespaces,
    self._group, self._version, self._kind,
    resource_version=list_resource_version,
):
    event_type = event["type"]  # ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED
    obj = event["object"]
    # update your cache
    ...

This is the standard list-then-watch pattern. No gap, no duplicates, no 410.

One thing you still need to handle: 410 can also happen legitimately during a long-running watch if etcd compacts past your last-seen version while you're watching. When that happens, you need to re-list and restart the watch. Standard retry loop:

async def run(self):
    while True:
        try:
            response = await api.list_custom_object_for_all_namespaces(
                self._group, self._version, self._kind
            )
            rv = response["metadata"]["resourceVersion"]
            self._cache = {item["metadata"]["name"]: item for item in response["items"]}
            self._ready = True

            w = watch.Watch()
            async for event in w.stream(
                api.list_custom_object_for_all_namespaces,
                self._group, self._version, self._kind,
                resource_version=rv,
            ):
                self._handle_event(event)
                rv = event["object"]["metadata"]["resourceVersion"]

        except ApiException as e:
            if e.status == 410:
                # compacted out, re-list
                continue
            raise

This is exactly how every Kubernetes controller/informer works internally — list, watch from the list's resourceVersion, re-list on 410.

If you're on a recent enough cluster (1.27+), you can also pass resourceVersionMatch=NotOlderThan with resourceVersion="0" on the list call to let the API server serve from cache, which is faster for large clusters. But the core pattern above is what you need.

Q: CodeIgniter Call to a member function on a non-object in [library] A:

You have duplicate class names. The controller class name is Guest and the library class name is also Guest.

When CodeIgniter goes to load the Guest library, it will skip over it and log a debug message. https://github.com/bcit-ci/CodeIgniter/blob/develop/system/core/Loader.php#L1032

I suggest renaming your library to something else, Registration perhaps?
